Unit 1 of 10: Environmental Value Systems (EVSs)

Key ideas

  • Environmental value system (EVS): a worldview or paradigm that shapes how a person or society sees and responds to environmental issues.
  • An EVS is itself a system: inputs (education, culture, religion, media, family, economics) are processed into outputs (decisions, actions, policies, lifestyles).
  • Perspectives are shaped by EVSs, so two people can look at the same data (e.g. a dam proposal) and reach opposite conclusions.
  • Values are not right or wrong in themselves; the exam rewards you for identifying them and explaining their influence.

Worked examples

Example 1: A hydroelectric dam: an engineer may value cheap low-carbon power; a local fishing community may value river access and livelihoods; an ecologist may value intact fish migration routes.

Example 2: Inputs to a teenager's EVS: school ESS lessons, social media climate campaigns and a family farming business. Outputs: joins a climate strike, but also supports subsidies for the family farm.

Example 3: Indigenous communities often hold relational values: land is part of identity, not just a resource.

10-mark exam-style question

(a) Define the term environmental value system. [2]

(b) Outline two inputs that may shape an individual's EVS. [4]

(c) Explain how two stakeholders with different EVSs might respond to a proposed open-pit mine. [4]

Answers:

  • (a) A worldview/paradigm (A1) that shapes the way an individual or group perceives and evaluates environmental issues (A1).
  • (b) Education, e.g. ESS courses that stress limits to growth (R2); culture or religion, e.g. traditions of stewardship (R2). Accept media, family, economic status, political views.
  • (c) A mining company (technocentric) may emphasise jobs, tax revenue and technological restoration after closure (R2); a local conservation group (ecocentric) may oppose it because of habitat loss, water pollution and the intrinsic value of the landscape (R2).

Common mistakes

  1. Defining EVS as "what someone thinks about nature" without saying it is a framework/worldview.
  2. Listing inputs without examples.
  3. Judging a value as "wrong" instead of explaining its influence.
  4. Forgetting that societies, not just individuals, have EVSs.
  5. Ignoring that EVSs change over time.

Quick recall

  1. What does EVS stand for?
  2. Give two inputs into an EVS.
  3. Give two outputs of an EVS.
  4. Why is an EVS described as a system?
  5. Can two people with the same data reach different decisions?

Answers: 1) Environmental value system. 2) Education, culture (also media, religion, family). 3) Decisions, actions (also policies, lifestyle). 4) It has inputs that are processed into outputs. 5) Yes, because their values differ.
